summary: Describes an RFC 3933 experiment to let the IETF community try a broader set of tools for managing mailing lists, such as long-term suspensions, beyond those in RFCs 3683 and 3934. It is experimental.

plainLanguage.summary: RFC 4633 describes an 18-month experiment with additional ways to manage posting on IETF mailing lists. It sets limits on those procedures and requires public notice before they take effect.

questions: how long can the iesg suspend posting rights
subtitle: An experiment that broadened the IESG's options for managing IETF mailing lists.

tldr.problem: The RFC describes a gap between a 30-day posting suspension and a longer ban under the mailing-list rules then in effect.
tldr.mechanism: For an 18-month experiment, the IESG could approve other list-management procedures, including longer posting suspensions, for specified IETF mailing lists. The procedures had to be announced publicly in advance and could not prevent reading a list.
tldr.outcome: RFC 4633 is an Experimental process document updated by RFC 8717. Its text says the experiment was intended to inform future guidelines, not to become a permanent Best Current Practice in its current form.

today: RFC 4633 is an Experimental process document and is updated by RFC 8717. Its text describes an experiment intended to inform future guidelines, rather than a permanent Best Current Practice in its current form.

sections.title: The Gap the Experiment Addressed
sections.content:
The RFC reviews earlier rules for managing disruptive behavior on IETF mailing lists. RFC 3934 allowed a working-group chair to suspend posting rights for 30 days, while RFC 3683 provided a ban of at least one year.

The document describes a gap between those measures and proposes a process experiment. Its stated purpose is to let the community try a broader set of tools while considering longer-term guidelines.
sections.plainLanguage: The existing rules described a short suspension and a much longer ban. This memo tests whether additional options could help manage mailing lists.

sections.title: Which Lists the Experiment Covers
sections.content:
The definition includes the IETF list, lists used by current working groups, lists retained after a working group closes, and lists created to support an IETF procedure. It also includes lists hosted on systems operated on behalf of the IETF.

This definition makes the experiment apply beyond working-group lists alone. It covers the kinds of mailing lists described by the RFC's definition of an IETF mailing list.
sections.plainLanguage: The experiment applies to official IETF mailing lists, including lists outside active working groups. The RFC defines which lists count.

sections.title: The Experiment's Powers and Limits
sections.content:
For 18 months, the IESG could approve other mailing-list controls for a specified set of lists. These could include suspending an individual's ability to post for longer than 30 days, and the IESG could delegate authority to apply longer suspensions.

A procedure under the experiment could not suspend posting beyond the experiment period or limit anyone's ability to read a list. The IESG had to announce a procedure publicly at least 14 days before it took effect and publish active procedures in an easy-to-find place. Sanctions could be appealed under RFC 2026.
sections.plainLanguage: The IESG could approve additional posting controls for named lists during the experiment. It had to announce each procedure at least 14 days before it began, and readers kept access to the lists.

sections.title: Examples of Possible Procedures
sections.content:
The informative examples include a fixed suspension longer than 30 days. The IESG could also delegate authority to a list's managers to continue longer suspensions if disruptive behavior continued.

Another example would let managers of a specified set of lists act after an initial suspension. These are examples of possible procedures, not requirements that every list use them.
sections.plainLanguage: The examples show how the IESG might let list managers apply additional posting controls. The RFC presents them as possibilities, not mandatory rules.
